If a DNS query returns NXDOMAIN, does that mean the name is permanently absent and will never exist?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. RFC 1034 section 4.3.4 ('Negative response caching') and RFC 2308 ('Negative Caching of DNS Queries') specify that NXDOMAIN responses are cached for a finite TTL (derived from the authoritative zone's SOA MINIMUM field, capped by the resolver). The authoritative meaning at the time of the query is 'this name does not exist now,' valid for that TTL only. The name can come into existence later; subsequent queries after cache expiry will then resolve. Cite: RFC 1034 section 4.3.4; RFC 2308 section 5.<|eot_id|>

Does the C11 standard guarantee that sizeof(int) >= 2?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Yes. C11 section 5.2.4.2.1 defines INT_MIN <= -32767 and INT_MAX >= 32767, requiring int to represent values in [-32767, 32767]. A 16-bit two's-complement integer covers this range exactly, so any conforming implementation has sizeof(int) * CHAR_BIT >= 16. Since CHAR_BIT >= 8 (5.2.4.2.1), sizeof(int) >= 2 follows. Cite: ISO/IEC 9899:2011 5.2.4.2.1.<|eot_id|>

When a POSIX process calls fork(), are the parent's open file descriptors duplicated into the child?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Yes. POSIX.1-2017 System Interfaces / fork: 'The child process shall have its own copy of the parent's file descriptors. Each of the child's file descriptors shall refer to the same open file description with the corresponding file descriptor of the parent.' So the descriptor numbers are duplicated in the child, but parent and child share the underlying open file description (meaning the file offset and status flags are shared, not independent). Cite: POSIX.1-2017, System Interfaces / fork.<|eot_id|>
